analysis.one_liner: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on June 16, 2026 and referred to the Finance Committee, which has taken no further action; no vote has been held.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations currently pay a 1% federal excise tax when they repurchase their own stock. This bill would raise that tax to 4% and close one of its offsets: companies could no longer reduce the tax by netting out stock reissued to top executives or to employees paid more than $1 million a year. The bill was introduced by the Senate Democratic leader with seven Democratic cosponsors and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the federal Treasury would collect more from large public companies that buy back their own stock, easing the tax burden on everyone else. The bill also targets a practice critics say channels corporate cash to shareholders and executives rather than workers or investment. [S1] [S2]

how_it_helps.text: The bill quadruples the 1% excise tax on stock repurchases to 4%, applying to repurchases after enactment. [S2]

It narrows the tax's offset so that stock reissued to covered executives or to anyone paid more than $1 million in a year no longer reduces the amount owed, meaning buybacks paired with executive equity pay no longer escape part of the tax. [S2]
Higher revenue from the tax reduces the need to raise other taxes or add to deficits, a benefit spread across ordinary taxpayers. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded corporations and their shareholders would pay more. Shareholders include ordinary people through retirement accounts, though most buyback activity is concentrated among the biggest firms and their largest investors. Executives and highly paid employees would lose the equity-issuance offset that currently reduces buyback tax bills. [S2]
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public companies and their investors

drawbacks.text: A 4% tax on repurchases is paid by the corporation, but economists generally agree some of it lands on shareholders through lower stock values, including the 401(k) and pension holders who own much of the market. [S2]
Companies can legally substitute dividends or debt-financed payouts for buybacks, so the tax changes how capital is returned rather than guaranteeing any of it goes to wages or investment. [S2]
The bill raises the rate and narrows an offset but does not restrict buybacks themselves or direct the revenue to any specific public purpose. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill raises a modest tax on a concentrated activity, with the burden falling mainly on big corporations, their large shareholders, and highly paid executives, while the revenue gain is spread across all taxpayers. The cost to ordinary retirement savers is real but small, since the tax is 4% of repurchases, not of the whole market. It is a narrow tax increase, not a ban or a redirect of corporate cash to workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it, and with no cosponsor from the Senate majority it is very unlikely to reach a vote before the session ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 16, 2026 by Sen. Schumer with Sens. Wyden, Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, and Whitehouse. [S1] [S2]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, with no subsequent action listed. [S4] [S1]
Seven Democratic senators cosponsored it; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors. [S3]
The Senate has 55 Republicans and 45 Democrats plus 2 independents, so a bill with only Democratic sponsorship has no evident majority coalition. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies and their biggest shareholders keep paying the 1% buyback tax instead of 4%, and highly paid executives keep the equity-issuance offset that reduces their companies' tax bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big corporations and their large shareholders

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and became its lead sponsor. [S1] [S4]

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and with Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats the bill has no evident path to a floor vote. [S3]

industries.note: The bill quadruples the excise tax they pay on buybacks and removes an offset tied to executive equity pay. [S2]

industries.industry: Corporate executives and employees earning over $1 million
industries.note: Their stock awards can no longer be netted against the buyback tax, raising the cost of buyback-plus-reissue pay strategies. [S2]
Some of the higher tax is expected to land on stock values, though revenue accrues to the Treasury rather than to private interests. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no Republican support and no scheduled action. With Republicans controlling the Senate 55 to 47, a standalone Democratic tax increase on buybacks is unlikely to get a committee markup or a floor vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Its only realistic paths are attachment to a broader tax or reconciliation package, which has not been signaled. [S1] [S4] [S3]
